content:
This week Michael Taylor, Associate Professor of History at SUNY Albany returns with a real treat: a transhistorical primer on combined arms warfare – why it matters, why it is hard and how it is done – stretching from the very early Iron Age to the present. Combined arms is one of those concepts that gets name-checked a lot in treatments of historical armies, but is far more rarely defined and discussed in detail, yet the devil is in the details – the actual mechanics that make an army more than the sum of its parts.
And with that, over to Michael…

One of the most difficult tasks for an army to accomplish is combined arms operations, the integration of different types of troops working together on the battlespace to accomplish a shared tactical and operational task. For most of pre-modernity, combined arms operations involved coordinating between cavalry, heavy infantry and light infantry. Potentially there were different sub-divisions within these basic types, for example heavily armored cataphracts and horse archers are both cavalry, but in fact fight quite differently: a cataphract makes a shock charge directly into the enemy while a horse archer shoots on the move, often flitting in and out of range from the enemy. Similarly, light infantry as a category might contain multitudes: slingers, archers, javelineers, etc. Heavy infantry, defined here as infantry with sufficient armor or shielding to hold a position, might have subtle gradations as well: for example in a Roman manipular legion the distinction between hastati and principes armed with heavy javelins (pila) and triarii armed with thrusting spears. In modern times, combined arms refers to coordination between the combat arms branches of infantry, artillery, armor (including “cavalry” scouts in armored vehicles) along with combat aviation assets like attack helicopters. These in turn are supported by combat support (engineers, ordinance, etc.) and combat service support units (logistics, medical asssets, civil affairs etc.).

In modern military parlance, Combined Arms refers to operations within services, while activities that involve assets from across the services (i.e. Army, Navy, Air Force, Marines and now, heavens help us, the Space Force) are referred to as Joint Operations. As an additional wrinkle, common across time will be what today would be called Combined/Joint Multinational Operations which involve allied countries. Most armies, particularly for large imperial states, were also multi-ethnic, so that facilitating combined arms meant not just integrating cavalry and light infantry, but doing so with light infantry and cavalry units that spoke different languages and practiced very different martial traditions and institutional cultures.

Challenges

Combined arms operations when done well provide diverse, mutually complimentary ways of engaging the enemy. Unfortunately, combined arms operations are quite difficult to do well. It is worth considering at least a few reasons why:

Combat mechanics: The main reason combined arms is hard is that fighting styles are often incompatible, or at least difficult to deconflict. Cavalry will advance faster than infantry. Light infantry can advance and retire faster than heavy infantry, but cannot hold ground when challenged in close combat. Heavy infantry need to maintain formation to maximize weapons reach and the mutual protection of shields, while light infantry swarm. Such differences will only be dramatically more complicated in modern combined arms, where the disparities between a tank, a mobile artillery piece and a groundpounding infantrymen will be even more profound. Simple questions, like should a tank have a telephone in the back so that infantry can call in to talk to the crew (the M1 Abrams famously eschewed this until the TUSK updates of the Iraq War) have great tactical import.

Leadership. How do leaders know how to fight and coordinate the different arms under their command? Most leaders come up learning how to fight one way. Across pre-modernity, most aristocrats who became generals had previously served as cavalrymen, and need not have had a granular mastery of, say, heavy infantry tactics. Indeed, Kelly DeVries has argued that one aspect that made Joan of Arc an effective military leader was that as a peasant woman she deigned to chat with commoner artillerists and so accrued little insights about the new technology that France’s other chevalier-class marshals overlooked.1 Conversely, while George S. Patton cut his teeth as a pioneering tank officer in WWI, one is struck reading his memoirs how much thought and consideration he devoted to infantry combat.2 Modern officers likewise come up from serving as junior and mid-level officers in a particular branch, although the US Army recently combined the Armor and Infantry into a Maneuver branch to smooth the divide. Such specialization is often necessary and even inevitable, but it also means that senior leaders can have a certain myopia when it comes to combined arms operations.

Status: Not all types of soldier enjoy the same social status, both within the army itself and potentially in the society from which different soldiers are recruited from. For most of premodernity, cavalrymen had a dramatically higher status than infantrymen (both heavy and light), never more so than the armored knights of the European Middle Ages. Heavy infantry oftentimes claimed a higher status than light infantry, with the latter often provided either by poorer men or foreigners. As surprising as it may seem, American infantry during World War II held a surprisingly low status, with ambitious and higher aptitude volunteers leaning towards the Air Corps, Airborne status or USMC.3 This led to concerted attempts to improve the prestige of the infantry branch, including the introduction of the Combat Infantry Badge. In the 21st century, the extraordinarily high status of Special Forces rather reverses the historical trend, with elite light infantry fetishized over regular mechanized infantry, armor and artillery. Status differentials can lead to tensions and resentments that gum up effective combined arms operations. And they can also exacerbate all sorts of tactical pathologies: low status troops might be used as cannon fodder, or socially elite troops might be dispatched on high-profile missions they are in fact ill-suited for (for example the dismounted frontal assault of French knights at Agincourt).

Logistics: Different types of troops can have very different logistical needs. A modern tank platoon requires enormous quantities of fuel, ammunition, and a steady stream of specialized replacement parts, while an infantry platoon might have more mundane requirements for “beans, bullets and band-aids.” At some point in a combined arms operation, a logistical officer and commander must prove themselves familiar with the needs of various types of units. In antiquity, cavalry had considerable logistical requirements, as horses required large amounts of food and fodder and water. Providing missiles to premodern light infantry, be they arrows or sling bullets, was another high end logistical problem. Marcus Crassus suffered defeat Carrhae (53 BC) in no small part because the Parthian commander Surena had arranged a special camel convoy to resupply his horse archers, dismaying the legionaries who had hoped (not entirely without reason) the enemy would just run out of arrows.4 The English state during the Hundred Years War likewise became quite adept at maintaining a centralized arrow supply that undergird its famous victories.

Related to status, some types of troops simply cost more, which can lead to penny pinching when it comes to deploying the optimal density of certain arms. In premodernity, the high status of cavalrymen, combined with the logistical requirements of maintaining horses, meant that cavalrymen simply cost much more.5 A Roman cavalryman during the Republic was paid three times that of an infantryman. In Medieval England, a common foot archer was paid about 2-3 pence a day, while a knight received a full two shillings a day (24 pence). Cost differentials could also lead to tactical pathologies, for example by the later phases of the Hundred Years War the English tended to field too many archers and not enough men-at-arms, a sub-optimal composition in the field, given that archers were defenseless without a bulwark of men-at-arms, but far cheaper to maintain in garrison.

Spectrum differentials: combined arms operations focus on major theater wars. But major theater wars are often infrequent, and the interim substantial military activity can be devoted to garrison duties, counterinsurgency, or what might be called petit guerre, i.e. skirmishing, wars of posts, and other permutations of small-scale conflict. The troop composition for these more frequent operations is different from what is required for intensive hegemonic warfare. But frequent petit guerre also shapes the experiences of soldiers and leaders. The US Army realized in the 2010s that much of its combined arms muscle had atrophied in Iraq and Afghanistan, where infantry, armor and artillery units often were retooled to perform missions associated with light infantry or military police (for example convoy escort or foot patrols). The fetishization of Special Forces is a related phenomenon: SF is a type of light infantry very useful in counterinsurgency and counterterrorism even if too delicate to be anything under than a supporting asset in a major theater war, all the while siphoning talented and ambitious soldiers away from line units.

With Our Arms Combined

Ultimately combined arms is very hard to do, with many structural factors militating towards sub-optimal performance. So how do successful armies manage combined arms well? Perhaps the biggest question for a force structure is what organizational level to integrate combined arms operations? Three basic options present themselves: 1) integration at the small unit level (e.g. squads, platoons or companies; 2) integration at the level of the primary tactical echelon (e.g. brigades or divisions) and 3) integration at the army-level.

Small Unit Integration: During World War II it was quite effective to attach a tank or tank destroyer to support an advancing infantry platoon or company, thus integrating armor and infantry at the small unit level. In some instances during street fighting, individual artillery pieces were even used to blast out positions to allow infantry platoons to advance. In sub-state or weak-state armies constituted on a “retinue of retinues” model, the retinue itself is often a combined arms reflecting mobilization along social hierarchies all beholden to the retinue leader. During the European High Middle Ages, a knight’s banner might include the knight himself, perhaps with two or three other mounted men-at-arms of equal or near-equal status (serjeants, gros valets, squires, etc.) along with a handful of dependents who served as infantry or archers. This was essentially a combined arms squad. Since this is a Tolkien friendly zone,6 it might be noted that the Fellowship of the Ring is precisely such a Medieval combined arms retinue, with a leader (Gandalf), two men-at-arms (Boromir, Strider), an archer (Legolas) a shock infantryman (Gimli) and four, er, very light footmen. Looking back to antiquity, the enigmatic Celtic trimarkisia may have functioned on a similar principle, with a mounted aristocratic warrior bringing along two subordinates who could fight on foot or mounted as the circumstances dictated.7 Archaic Greek hoplite warfare, where seventh century BC hoplites fought intermixed with light infantry and archers, likely functioned on a similar social basis, with a wealthy man fighting with armor and large aspis shields flanked by his lightly armed dependents, while the wealthiest flexed across the battlefield in their chariots. The informal pairing in the Iliad (which may reflect awareness of more formal Assyrian combined arms tactics practiced at the time of the poem’s composition) of Greater Ajax and his brother Teucer, whereby Teucer shoots his bow from behind his brother’s tower shield, envisions an informal combined arms strategy at the level of the buddy team, although in the Iliad it is hinted they work well together not simply because they are of the same noble status, but because of their brotherly bond.8

More formal attempts to integrate archers and shieldmen at the level of the infantry file can be seen by the Assyrians, the first great state army of the Iron Age. Assyrian shieldmen and archers are often depicted fighting in pairs, with spear-armed shieldmen protecting the archer. Assyrian heavy infantry and archers could also segregate, for example during the final assault of a city, with heavy infantrymen scaling ladders while the archers lay down a base of “fire.”9 The Achaemenid Persians seem to have largely continued the practice of mixing different types of soldiers within a single infantry file, although they deepened the file beyond the Assyrian pairing, so that a shieldman, sometimes with a large spara shields protected several ranks of archers, who themselves could also fight with spears, shields and swords once they ran out of arrows, that is double as both light and line infantry.10 Indeed, having soldiers wear two hats as both light and heavy infantry was a not uncommon, if not always successful solution across history.

Yet experience increasingly showed that uniform formations of heavy infantry was the best way to maximize both the protective qualities of shields and armor, and also the shock value of the infantry assault. Imagine a simplified combat scenario where a heavily armed infantryman is fighting next to an archer. If this pair is attacked by two opposing heavily armed infantrymen (whose shields and armor have deflected the archer’s arrows) then the most likely result is the archer is quickly killed and the surviving footman now faces two opponents. Better to have a line of just hoplites. By the fifth century BC, and probably earlier, light troops were kicked out of the hoplite phalanx, which became a pure heavy infantry formation. On the Achaemenid side, it seems that some units had always fought primarily as spearmen, but by the fourth century BC the Achaemenids were making use of Greek-style hoplite formations, sometimes employing Greek mercenaries or sometimes their own subjects, like the Lycians on the Xanthus reliefs, further substituting at least some of their mixed shieldman/archer formations with more uniform heavy infantry.

Army Level Integration: Thus in the ancient Greek world by the Classical period the most common echelon of combined arms integration was the army itself. No sub-unit contained a mix of light infantry, cavalry, and heavy infantry, but the commanding general managed the tactical interaction of major units of different arms as part of the grand battle plan. Generals levying armies needed to ensure their overall force had the proper mix of hoplites, cavalry and light infantry (psiloi). In battle, a recurring solution across antiquity was to place heavy infantry in the center, screened to the front or flanks by light troops, with cavalry posted on the flanks where they could maneuver. But coordinating amongst these still required a deft touch. The early fourth century BC Athenian commander Iphicrates supposedly likened the ideal combined arms integration of an army to the human body: the peltasts supply the hands, the cavalry the feet, the hoplites the cuirassed chest, and the general himself the head coordinating the activity of the congruent parts.11 Notably, Iphicrates considered combined arms integration the primary task of the general. Iphicrates himself was responsible for improving the quality of Athenian light infantry, both in terms of their equipment, including the use of a Thracian style center grip shield, the pelte, and through recruiting peltasts from wealthier men who had traditionally served as hoplites––that is raising the social status of light infantry service as a means of increasing its tactical salience. Iphicrates inflicted a devastating defeat on a group of Spartan hoplites at Lechaion in 391 BC, when these made the mistake of trying to move in open country without light infantry or cavalry screens, only to suffer devastating attrition by hit-and-run tactics from the new peltast force.12 The beleaguered Spartan commander also did not know how to utilize the cavalry that eventually came to his aid, retaining them alongside his hoplites, rather than allowing them to charge ahead to decisively disrupt the hit-and-run sequence. It may well be that the Spartan commander, socialized in the peculiar Spartan system of square bashing,  simply suffered  “hoplite brain” and had not thought through the best way to deploy a cavalry asset.

Alexander the Great was arguably the most effective combined arms commanders of pre-modernity.13 His father, Philip II, had forged an army that combined heavy cavalry drawn from the traditional Macedonian aristocracy with a heavy infantry force of pikemen recruited from the free peasantry. To help tie-in the main pike phalanx in with the cavalry charge, Philip created a special unit of hypaspistai (“shield-bearers”), essentially swifter and perhaps somewhat more lightly armored phalangites who could surge forward to fill the gap between the cavalry charge and the more slowly advancing infantry. Of course, as discussed above, status differentials between arms branches can hinder effective cooperation. The traditional social status of Macedonian heavy cavalry was extremely high: cavalrymen saw themselves as “companions” hetairoi to the king. Philip could not promote perfect social equality, but he could smooth the disparity by raising the prestige of his pike infantry, dubbing them pezhetairoi “foot companions.” While the title of hypaspistai previously referred to a servant who carried a hoplite’s shield, Philip’s hypaspists saw themselves as collective shield-bearers to the king himself, a very lofty corporate status (late in Alexander’s reign, this unit would be given silver plated shields and rebranded as the argyaspides, further attesting to their high status). As Macedonia’s hegemony waxed, and the army was supplemented by foreign subjects and subaltern allies, ethnic solidarity as Makedones proved an important force binding together the core one-two punch of pikemen and heavy cavalry.

Macedonian combined arms tactics worked in part because there was a standard operating procedure (SOP) for how the major pieces would operate together in pitched battle: the cavalry on the left would be refused (held back) while the center-right element would launch an echelon attack, with the cavalry on the right leading, the hypaspistai acting as a flexible connector and the phalanx advancing its mass at its own pace, screened by light skirmishers, who also helped protect the extreme flanks and rear of the formation. This SOP meant that the king as general did not have to spend a lot of time and bandwidth generating novel ways for his army to work together, and that the troops and their officers developed patterns of cooperation and communication. In this “Alexander Battle” combined-arms SOP, the king only had to make a few key decisions to effect the carefully determined plan: when and where to launch his cavalry charge (that is finding a weakness in the enemy line to exploit), and then when he should cut short his pursuit to roll up the main enemy line. Easier said than done, and the key to Alexander’s generalship was his immaculate coup d’oeil, his ability at a glance to assess the sweeping grand tactical situation and then strike at the most opportune moment (in Greek the kairos) and location. Once Alexander had made his determination, he could steer his entire combined arms force by charging forward himself: where Alexander rode, he could be sure his elite bodyguards (somatophylakes) would follow, followed in turn by his hetairoi cavalry, themselves tethered to the main phalanx by the hypaspists. But a problem emerged once Alexander drank himself to death in Babylon: this combined arms plan required a brilliant and inspired commander to pull it off. Alexander’s successors imitated his style and continued to try and fight the Alexander battle, but without his praeternatural success. This problem has been diagnosed by Graham Wrightson, who in particular argues that the Seleucid king Antiochus III simply could not pull off Macedonian combined arms tactics with the same verve and flair.14

It is possible to diagnose particular things successor kings tended to do wrong. A common error was to over pursue on the cavalry charge, that is the king got too involved fighting a cavalry-on-cavalry action that he failed to pivot to fulfill the broader combined arms plan. This was the blunder of Demetrius Poliorcetes at Ipsus (301 BC), of Antiochus III at Raphia (217 BC) and of Antiochus III ( he just couldn’t quit) at Magnesia (190 BC).15 The seemingly simple things Alexander did were in fact quite hard. The Seleucid army in particular had the tendency to accrue a massive bric-a-brack of light infantry units, who cluttered the flanks without adding much to the main battle. But the larger issue was organizational. It is quite difficult to integrate combined arms at the level of the army, and integration at this level places extraordinary pressure on the general and his senior staff to ensure that all the various cogs and gears and widgets of the combined arms machine whirred smoothly. Indeed, integration at the army level depends on having a military genius as a general, and suffers from any commander’s feet of clay.

Primary division integration: There is a happy median between often chaotic small unit integration at the level of a retinue or platoon and integration at the level of the army. Arguably the most effective way to nest combined arms operations is at the level of the main subdivision of the army. This was how the US Army organized itself to fight World War II. Then the main sub-unit was the division of approximately 15,000 soldiers. Importantly, soldiers were encouraged to identify themselves corporately with their divisions. This was the unit patch that they wore on their right shoulders, and indeed if a soldier saw combat with a division, he was allowed to wear that patch on his left shoulder for the rest of his career. This corporate esprit d’ corps was important precisely because the division was a major locus for combined arms integration.

Of course, US divisions carried labels of “Infantry” or “Armor,” but in reality, to borrow a term from mixology, we might consider these “Infantry forward” or “Armor forward” combined arms divisions. Already during World War I, US infantry divisions had a regiment of artillery nested with (this was relatively standard international practice, it should be noted). But this is precisely what routine combined arms integration looks like: organic integration at the primary tactical unit. While a US infantry division did not have organic armor during World War II, the US Army maintained separate tank and tank destroyer battalions which could be attached to support particular infantry divisions. This arrangement was not without potential frictions, as the separate battalions risked becoming institutional orphans when it came to equipment and replacement personnel, although inertia often saw certain tank or TD battalions attached to a particular division for an extended period, which provided the possibility for the development of longer term working relationships, a semi-organic connection if you will. For example, the 743th Tank Battalion was attached to the 30th Infantry Division from June 14th 1944 to VE Day; the resulting combined arms element, nine infantry battalions, three artillery battalions, and a semi-organic tank battalion famously defeated a notorious German combined arms element, Kampfgruppe Peiper, along the Ambleve River during the opening phases of the Battle of the Bulge (Dec. 18th–24th, 1944). KG Pieper consisted of a medium panzer battalion, a heavy panzer battalion of Tigers, a battalion of mechanized infantry (panzergenadiers) and a towed artillery battalion. The face-off between a US infantry division with artillery and armor, and a German armored battlegroup with infantry and artillery demonstrates the extent that 20th century combined arms practice converged through institutional isomorphism.

American armored divisions during World War II meanwhile were an even more organic mix of tanks, mechanized infantry and mobile artillery. To break down institutional barriers to combined arms activity, US armored divisions were divided into three combat commands (CCA, CCB and a reserve CCR) which could be allotted a mix of tank, mechanized infantry and mobile artillery battalions. This principle (like a German Panzerkampfgruppe) allowed the division commander tremendous flexibility to mix and match combined arms capabilities to meet the mission, while soldiers retained their esprit d’corps at the level of the division even as their battalions and companies shuffled between Combat Commands. Indeed, this principle pointed to how the US army would organize itself going forward, eventually doing away with single-arms regiments, and making the Brigade (currently Brigade Combat Team, BCT) the primary level where combined arms integration occurred (constant tweaks are ongoing). If there is a flaw in the current BCT model, soldiers are still encouraged to identify with their umbrella Divisions and their august WWII heritage, even as combat arms integration is focused on the Brigade. The exception is the National Guard, where some old WWII divisions have been retooled as brigades, including the 30th Mobile Brigade Combat Team of the North Carolina National Guard, the legacy unit of the storied World War II division.

Combined arms at the level of a major tactical subdivision was relatively rare in the ancient world. A salient exception was the manipular legion of the Middle Republican Rome. This practice originated somewhat by accident. Early Rome had initially levied a single legion (the word legio just meant “levy”), which consisted of light troops, heavy infantry and aristocratic cavalry, the principle of combined arms integration at the level of the army. But in the mid-fourth century BC, probably as a result of the Licinio-Sextian reforms that created the classical consulship, the Romans doubled the levy so that each consul could command a single legion. By 311 BC, each consul was assigned two legions, so that a legion was now the most important subdivision of the Roman army; this also meant that combined arms was integrated at the level of the legion, which had 1200 light infantry (velites) 3000 heavy infantry (divided into three lines, triplex acies, of hastati, principes and triarii) and 300 cavalry.

While the cavalry was often detached to the wings in pitched battle, the different arms of the legion frequently worked hand-in-hand, both operationally during the  campaign and tactically during pitched battle. Velites guarded the camp perimeter during the day while the maniples rotated through the night-watch, supervised by the cavalry.16 In the marching column, cavalry either rode interspersed behind their organic infantry, or were brigaded to protect the baggage train, the most vulnerable part of the marching formation.17 Closing with the enemy, velites often accompanied the cavalry to skirmish and seize forward positions.18 In pitched battles, velites screened the front of the triplex acies as it formed its battleline while cavalry formed up to protect its vulnerable flanks. Once the triplex acies had broken the enemy formation, the cavalry pursued and massacred enemies in their flight.

The social boundaries between the different arms of the legion overlapped at the edges. Many heavy infantrymen in the triplex acies had initially served as velites before aging into heavy infantry service. Some of the wealthiest men in the infantry will have experienced service as both infantrymen and cavalrymen cum equis suis (men who provided their own horse, in contrast to aristocratic cavalry who were issued a public horse at state expense). It is notable that velites do not seem to be viewed as cannon fodder in the way that High Imperial authors would later view auxiliary cohorts fighting in front of the legions.19 Cavalrymen could even be called upon to labor digging ditches for siege works when necessary (although in one instance they were roundly punished for refusing to do so).20 Shared citizenship and social overlap eased some of the rivalries and social frictions that corrode the efficacy of combined arms operations.

Furthermore, subordinates below the level of the army commander could facilitate combined arms integration. The pairing of velites with cavalry troopers at Capua in 211 BC, where by the velites rode double and then leapt down to fight one foot, was facilitated by a legionary centurion named Quintus Navius.21 Military tribunes, the six elected officers who staffed each legion, had previously served as cavalrymen, but carried the light target-shield of the velites, the parma, and circulated, like the velites did, in between and to front of the heavy-infantry maniples. The organic position of light infantry was particularly integral to manipular tactics, where the matrix of heavy infantry was screened and maintained by the pulse of velites in and out of the manipular checkerboard. Roman commanders could and did detach light infantry and cavalry elements as their battle plan required. But this detachment had to be the conscious choice of the commander. Combined arms integration was the default setting for the legion, something it did well even if the commander failed to put much thought into it.

Perplexingly, after Rome succeeded in conquering the Mediterranean, it dismantled the legion as a combined arms force. The legions of Julius Caesar’s Commentaries (c. 58–44 BC) are composed entirely of cohorts of heavy infantry, supported by inorganic cavalry and light infantry provided by Gallic and Germanic allies. It took Caesar’s genius to make this work well. While some citizens would later serve in legionary cavalry during the civil wars, and it is possible that some citizen light infantry units also persisted, the organic combined arms of the Middle Republican legion was clearly a thing of the past by the Late Republic. Why should this be?

We can only speculate, but costs and logistics may have played a role. A single horse can take up as much space on a boat as five men.22 Roman commanders may have preferred to rely on auxiliary light infantry and cavalry which could be recruited in the theater, and often paid for by subject communities. Comparative advantage may have played a role as well, as Rome acquired subjects who were better light infantry (like Balearic slingers) and cavalry (such as the Numidians and Gauls). The downside was that while a Numidian horseman or Balearic slinger might be a better man-for-man than a Roman eques or veles, the advantages of a combined arms legion were lost. Indeed, now barriers of language, culture and legal status stood between combined arms activity. Furthermore, there is evidence that heavy Roman legionaries were often forced to be their own light infantry: Caesar maintained special troops called antesignani who were capable of dashing forward to seize forward positions.23 Caesar himself criticized Pompeian legionaries for surging forward in a loose and haphazard fashion but they likely advanced in a swarm like the velites once did precisely because they had no light infantry do so instead.24 The legion-level production of sling bullets in the Late Republic raises the question of who was doing the slinging, and the most obvious default was that some legionaries were forward deployed to serve as slingers, perhaps before falling back into their cohorts for pitched combat.25 This was far from ideal, and notably, the Roman army clawed some combined arms organization in the early imperial period, with each legion regaining about 125 cavalrymen, while a number of auxiliary cohortes equitanae functioned as combined arms battalions, mixing of six centuries of infantry (480 foot) and four turmae of cavalry (120 riders).

Interestingly, the reception of the Roman legion in the 18th century was very much as a model of combined arms combat. Afterall, schoolboys after a few sound whippings26 could read their Livy and Polybius and learn that the legion was an empire building combination of infantry, lights and cavalry. As modern combined arms developed, a “legion” became the term for a unit that combined regular line infantry, skirmishers like riflemen, field artillery, dragoons (mounted infantry) and regular cavalry. This can be seen in the history of the Revolutionary War, where the infamous Banastre Tarleton commanded the British Legion, composed of loyalist Americans, a somewhat chaotic mix of infantry and dragoons, mostly famous for committing war crimes. In the 1790s, the new nation itself raised the Legion of the United States after set-backs in early attempts to ethnically cleanse the Ohio Valley in the 1790s. Authorized at a classically resonant paper strength of 4000 troops, the Legion of the United States integrated line infantry, riflemen skirmishers, dragoons and artillery companies. None of these “legions” sought to strictly replicate the tactical organization of the Roman legion, in terms of maniples, cohorts or the triplex acies. But the emulation nonetheless went deeper than just cribbing the name, and in fact reflected a sensitive reading of military history: the Roman legion had proved dominant not necessarily because of ineffable factors like the genius of its generals or even the valor of its soldiers, but because of the practical matter that it was the institutional locus for organic combined arms integration.
